desc:
Split the string s into k non-empty consecutive pieces a1, a2, ..., ak (so that s = a1a2...ak) such that the sequence of pieces reads the same from both sides: ai = ak+1-i for every i. (When k is odd, the middle piece is compared with itself.)

Return the largest possible k. Note that k = 1 (the whole string as a single piece) is always allowed.

For example, "abcxyzabc" gives 3 (abc | xyz | abc); "aaaa" gives 4; "abcab" gives 3 (ab | c | ab); "abcd" gives 1.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Try a recursive formulation: choose the first piece, which forces the last piece to be the same string, and recurse on what is left between them.
Is it ever worse to cut the shortest possible matching piece (prefix equal to the suffix at the other end) than a longer one?

Greedy: grow a candidate prefix length one letter at a time and compare it to the suffix of the same length at the other end of the remaining part. The first time they are equal, cut both pieces (count 2) and restart on the inside. A remaining non-empty middle with no match counts as one piece.
editorial: Let y be the shortest string that is both a prefix and a suffix of the remaining part (non-overlapping). Suppose an optimal decomposition starts with a longer first piece x; then x is also a prefix and a suffix of the remaining part, and so is its shortest border, which is a match of length at most |x| / 2. That match cannot be shorter than y, so y itself is a border of x and x = y w y for some (possibly empty) w. Replacing the outer pair x ... x by y | w | y ... y | w | y gives a valid decomposition with more pieces, a contradiction. Hence an optimal decomposition always starts with y, and the greedy choice of the shortest match is safe.

Implementation: keep the remaining range [lo, hi) and a length L growing from 1. When s[lo:lo+L] == s[hi-L:hi], add 2, shrink the range by L on both sides and reset L. If the range becomes too short to hold two pieces of length L, whatever is left (if anything) is one middle piece and adds 1. Every letter is covered by the slices of at most one growing attempt, so slice comparisons cost O(n2) in the worst case with plain slicing (fast in C for these limits) and O(n) with a rolling hash.
time: O(n^2) worst case, O(n) with hashing
solution:
def maxMirrorChunks(s):
    n = len(s)
    lo, hi = 0, n
    count = 0
    L = 1
    while hi - lo > 0:
        if 2 * L > hi - lo:
            count += 1
            break
        if s[lo:lo + L] == s[hi - L:hi]:
            count += 2
            lo += L
            hi -= L
            L = 1
        else:
            L += 1
    return count
